USMLE-style practice · Pharmacology

Low systemic exposure

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

In a pharmacokinetic study, an orally administered ulcer-protective agent remains predominantly in the gastrointestinal tract while improving mucosal healing. Which property best fits sucralfate and distinguishes it from a systemically absorbed receptor antagonist?

  1. It acts by increasing serum gastrin
  2. Its therapeutic action is mainly local
  3. It must enter the brain before acting
  4. It requires hepatic CYP activation to block H2 receptors
  5. It accumulates in parietal-cell canaliculi as an active sulfenamide
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Its therapeutic action is mainly local

Sucralfate acts mainly at the mucosal surface and is only minimally absorbed.

Understanding the options

Its therapeutic action is mainly local
Sucralfate acts mainly at the mucosal surface and is only minimally absorbed.
It must enter the brain before acting
CNS entry is unnecessary.
It requires hepatic CYP activation to block H2 receptors
It does not act as an activated H2 antagonist.
It accumulates in parietal-cell canaliculi as an active sulfenamide
Active sulfenamide formation is characteristic of PPIs.
It acts by increasing serum gastrin
Raising serum gastrin is not its therapeutic mechanism.
